claim_feeding_always_pollinates_label: Every nectar visit transfers pollen to the next flower
claim_feeding_always_pollinates_why: Your recorded visits compare the same flowers with and without contact. Pollen reached the receptive surface when contact occurred; the butterfly still sipped nectar when contact was missed, but no pollen transferred. Feeding alone does not establish pollination.
claim_green_enough_label: Any green, planted patch will do
claim_green_enough_why: The mown lawn and the flowering bergamot are both green and planted, and neither fed a monarch caterpillar. What matters is which species are growing, not how green the patch looks.
claim_nectar_enough_label: Flowers with nectar are enough to support monarchs here
claim_nectar_enough_why: Nectar feeds the adult stage you fly. Every generation you followed on a nectar-only patch stopped at the caterpillar stage, which needs milkweed leaves.
claim_needs_both_label: Monarchs need nectar for adults and milkweed for caterpillars
claim_needs_both_why: Adults refuel at any flowering patch, but only patches with milkweed leaves carried a generation through the caterpillar stage to an adult.
claim_next_green_enough: To test whether any green patch will do, follow a generation on Mown lawn or Wild bergamot and record the result.
claim_next_nectar_enough: To test nectar alone, follow a generation on Wild bergamot or a bergamot-only restoration plot and record the result.
claim_next_needs_both_host: Next, follow a generation on Common milkweed or a milkweed + bergamot restoration plot and record the result. You already have a nectar-only comparison.
claim_next_needs_both_nectar: Next, follow a generation on Wild bergamot or a bergamot-only restoration plot and record the result. A milkweed success alone does not test whether nectar could substitute for host leaves.
claim_next_needs_both_neither: To compare the stages' needs, follow a generation on Common milkweed and another on Wild bergamot, then record both results.
claim_next_pollination: At the same flowering patch and planting, finish and record two model flower visits: one touching the receptive surface and one missing it. Use the final visit step at 100% progress, then Record this flower visit for each case.
claim_next_season: To test timing, run the SAME patch twice under different mowing plans: leave a milkweed patch uncut, then cut it before the caterpillar or chrysalis stage.
claim_timing_irrelevant_label: If the right plants are there, when the patch is mown does not matter
claim_timing_irrelevant_why: You ran the same patch, with the same plants, under two mowing plans and got two different outcomes. A cut that lands before a stage needs the plant removes it just as surely as never planting it.
claim_verdict_unsupported: Your records do not support that claim.
claim_verdict_untested: You have not tested this claim yet.

data_design_flowers_detail: A flowering patch of Monarda fistulosa
data_design_flowers_note: Flowering bergamot provides adult nectar. Monarch caterpillars still need milkweed leaves, which are absent from this design.
data_design_flowers_note_simple: Bergamot gives butterflies nectar. But there is no milkweed for caterpillars.
data_design_lawn_detail: Short mown grass, as the plot is today
data_design_lawn_note: The mown restoration plot has no nectar flowers or milkweed leaves. Neither resource is present in this design.
data_design_lawn_note_simple: Short grass only: no flowers and no milkweed.
data_design_mixed_detail: Both species, established and in bloom
data_design_mixed_note: This planting offers adult nectar and milkweed leaves for monarch caterpillars. Having both resources does not guarantee survival.
data_design_mixed_note_simple: This has nectar for butterflies and milkweed for caterpillars. Having both still does not promise that every monarch lives.
data_mowing_early_note: An early cut removes the milkweed leaves a caterpillar would have fed on.
data_mowing_early_note_simple: An early cut takes away the milkweed leaves the caterpillars need.
data_mowing_late_note: By this point the adult has emerged and can leave, so this cut does not interrupt the generation.
data_mowing_late_note_simple: By then the butterfly has come out and can fly away, so this cut does no harm.
data_mowing_mid_note: This model keeps the chrysalis inside the patch. A midsummer cut removes its support; real caterpillars often leave their milkweed plant to find a secure pupation site.
data_mowing_mid_note_simple: A midsummer cut takes away the plants the chrysalis hangs on. (Real caterpillars often crawl away to make their chrysalis.)
data_mowing_never_note: Nothing is cut, so whatever grows here stays standing for the whole generation.
data_mowing_never_note_simple: Nothing is mowed, so the plants stay all summer.
data_plant_bergamot_note: Flowering wild bergamot offers nectar for adult monarchs. It does not replace milkweed as food for monarch caterpillars.
data_plant_bergamot_note_simple: Butterflies drink nectar from bergamot flowers. Caterpillars cannot eat bergamot.
data_plant_lawn_latin: A patch with no flowers or milkweed
data_plant_lawn_note: This mown patch has neither flowers for nectar nor milkweed leaves for monarch caterpillars. That describes this patch, not every lawn.
data_plant_lawn_note_simple: This short grass has no flowers and no milkweed. (Some lawns do have flowers.)
data_plant_milkweed_note: Milkweed provides leaves for monarch caterpillars. When in bloom, its flowers also offer nectar to adults.
data_plant_milkweed_note_simple: Caterpillars eat milkweed leaves. Butterflies drink nectar from its flowers.
data_stage_adult_caption: The adult emerges and feeds on flower nectar — the stage you fly.
data_stage_adult_caption_simple: The butterfly comes out and drinks nectar from flowers. You fly this stage.
data_stage_adult_failing: No adult emerges from this patch this generation.
data_stage_adult_failing_simple: No butterfly comes out of this patch this time.
data_stage_adult_thriving: An adult emerges. From here it can fly to nectar flowers — in this patch or any other — the way you do.
data_stage_adult_thriving_simple: A butterfly comes out! It can fly to any flowers for nectar, just like you.
data_stage_caterpillar_caption: The caterpillar feeds and grows. This is the stage that depends on milkweed leaves.
data_stage_caterpillar_caption_simple: The caterpillar eats and grows. It needs milkweed leaves.
data_stage_caterpillar_failing: The caterpillar hatched with no milkweed leaves within reach. Nectar flowers are adult food and do not feed this stage; the generation does not continue here.
data_stage_caterpillar_failing_simple: The caterpillar has no milkweed to eat. Flowers feed butterflies, not caterpillars. The life cycle stops here.
data_stage_caterpillar_thriving: The caterpillar is feeding on milkweed leaves and growing through its larval stage.
data_stage_caterpillar_thriving_simple: The caterpillar is eating milkweed leaves and growing bigger.
data_stage_chrysalis_caption: The caterpillar forms a chrysalis and reorganizes into an adult.
data_stage_chrysalis_caption_simple: The caterpillar makes a chrysalis. Inside, it changes into a butterfly.
data_stage_chrysalis_failing: No caterpillar completed feeding at this patch, so no chrysalis forms.
data_stage_chrysalis_failing_simple: No caterpillar could finish eating here, so there is no chrysalis.
data_stage_chrysalis_thriving: A caterpillar that fed well forms its chrysalis, where metamorphosis takes place.
data_stage_chrysalis_thriving_simple: The well-fed caterpillar makes its chrysalis and starts to change.
data_stage_egg_caption: A monarch egg is laid on a leaf. It does not feed yet; what matters is the plant it sits on.
data_stage_egg_caption_simple: A tiny egg is laid on a leaf. It does not eat. What matters is which plant it is on.
data_stage_egg_failing: The egg is on a plant with no milkweed leaves. It can still hatch, but no monarch caterpillar food is growing here.
data_stage_egg_failing_simple: The egg is not on milkweed. It can still hatch, but there is no food here for the caterpillar.
data_stage_egg_thriving: The egg rests on a milkweed leaf. When it hatches, the caterpillar will emerge onto its food plant.
data_stage_egg_thriving_simple: The egg is on a milkweed leaf. When it hatches, the caterpillar will be right on its food.

fact_feet_text: A female drums her feet on a leaf to taste it and check that it is milkweed. She usually lays one egg at a time, often on the underside of a leaf.
fact_feet_text_simple: A mother monarch tastes leaves with her feet! She checks that a leaf is milkweed before she lays an egg under it.
fact_growth_text: In about two weeks, a caterpillar grows to almost 2,000 times as heavy as when it hatched. It sheds its too-tight skin between five stages called instars.
fact_growth_text_simple: In about two weeks, a caterpillar gets almost 2,000 times heavier! It grows through five stages, and between them it sheds its too-tight skin.
fact_lifespan_text: Most summer monarchs live about 2 to 5 weeks as butterflies. The last generation of the year migrates south and can live up to 8 or 9 months.
fact_lifespan_text_simple: Most summer butterflies live about 2 to 5 weeks. The last ones of the year fly south and can live 8 or 9 months.
fact_time_text: In summer, egg to butterfly takes about a month: about 3–5 days as an egg, about 2 weeks as a caterpillar and 1–2 weeks as a chrysalis. Cool weather slows it down.
fact_time_text_simple: In summer, it takes about a month to go from egg to butterfly. Cool weather makes it slower.
feed_out_arrived: The butterfly has arrived. Watch for contact with the receptive surface.
feed_out_carry: Pollen is traveling on the butterfly. The next flower has received none yet.
feed_out_no_contact: No pollen reaches the receptive surface in this visit. The butterfly keeps its pollen while sipping nectar.
feed_out_received_bergamot: Some grains have reached the receptive stigma. Other grains remain on the butterfly.
feed_out_received_milkweed: One pollinium has entered the receptive slit. The other remains on the butterfly.
feed_out_sip_attached: Pollen has attached to the butterfly during its nectar visit.
feed_out_sip_reaching: The drinking tube is reaching into the flower; pollen has not attached yet.
feed_out_transferring: Watch the pollen move from the leg toward the receptive surface. It is still in transfer.
feed_phase_carry_note: Pollen rides on the outside of the butterfly as it visits another flower of the same plant species. Nectar stays inside the butterfly as food.
feed_phase_deposit_note: Contact leaves some pollen on a receptive flower surface. This transfer is pollination. Fertilization and seed development can follow later; a visit alone does not guarantee seeds.
feed_phase_miss_note: The butterfly can reach nectar, but its pollen misses the receptive surface. In this comparison, the pollen stays on the butterfly. Feeding and pollination are different events.
feed_phase_sip_note: The proboscis is a long, flexible drinking tube. It uncoils to reach sugary nectar inside the flower. Pollen attaches outside the body during contact; it is not the nectar being swallowed.

fw_cases_count: {value1} of 2 cases recorded at this patch. Keep the flowers the same and change only contact.

fw_contact_help: Compare the receptive surface in or outside the pollen path. Both flowers are the same plant species.
fw_help_bergamot: Bergamot has tubular flowers. Loose pollen grains can brush onto the butterfly and reach a receptive stigma on another bergamot flower. Compare contact and missed contact in the final step.
fw_help_milkweed: Milkweed packages its pollen in paired pollinia. A packet can catch on a leg and enter a receptive slit in another milkweed flower. Compare contact and missed contact in the final step.

fw_pollen_fact: Did you know? Butterflies stand high on long, thin legs, so less pollen sticks to them than to bees, which gather pollen on purpose. Contact is never guaranteed. (USDA Forest Service)

gl_help: Each entry says what the word means in general, then how this lab uses it.
gl_summary: Glossary · {value1} words used in this lab
gloss_chrysalis_definition: The stage inside which a caterpillar reorganizes into an adult butterfly. It hangs from a stem or other support and does not feed.
gloss_chrysalis_here: This model places the chrysalis inside the patch and assumes mowing removes its support. Real caterpillars often leave their milkweed plant to find a secure place to pupate.
gloss_evidence_definition: A record of something you observed, which can support or contradict a claim. What you did not observe is not evidence, however reasonable it sounds.
gloss_evidence_here: The claim panel counts patches you examined, generations and seasons you recorded, and flower visits you explicitly recorded.
gloss_generation_definition: One round of the life cycle, from eggs laid to the adults that emerge from them.
gloss_generation_here: "Follow a generation" tracks one of these on a patch you have examined.
gloss_habitat_restoration_definition: Planting or managing land so it provides what a species needs. For monarchs that means milkweed for caterpillars and nectar flowers for adults, protected from things like poorly timed mowing.
gloss_habitat_restoration_here: The fourth patch is yours to restore. Each plan changes what the plot offers.
gloss_host_plant_definition: The plant a caterpillar can actually eat. Female monarchs lay eggs on milkweed because monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed. A plant can be full of flowers and still not be a host plant.
gloss_host_plant_here: In this lab, "milkweed leaves present" is what makes a patch a host plant for monarchs.
gloss_instar_definition: One growth step between two molts. A monarch caterpillar passes through five instars, getting larger at each.
gloss_instar_here: The lab shows the caterpillar as one step. Instars are what that single step is made of.
gloss_larva_definition: The feeding and growing stage that hatches from the egg. A monarch caterpillar grows through five stages, shedding its skin between them.
gloss_larva_here: This is the stage that stops a generation when no milkweed is within reach.
gloss_metamorphosis_definition: The whole change from egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to adult, in which the animal is rebuilt rather than simply growing bigger.
gloss_metamorphosis_here: Following a generation walks through these four stages in order.
gloss_milkweed_definition: The group of plants (genus Asclepias) that monarch caterpillars depend on. Its flowers also offer nectar, so milkweed can serve both the adult and the caterpillar.
gloss_milkweed_here: Common milkweed (Asclepias syriaca) is the one patch here that provides both resources.
gloss_nectar_plant_definition: A flowering plant whose nectar feeds adult butterflies. Nectar fuels flight and egg-laying, but it is not food for caterpillars.
gloss_nectar_plant_here: Examining a flowering patch refills your flight energy meter. That is the adult stage feeding.
gloss_pollen_definition: Material produced by a flower’s anthers that carries the male reproductive cells of the plant. It is different from nectar, the liquid food the adult butterfly drinks.
gloss_pollen_here: The enlarged yellow grains or packets ride outside the butterfly. Compare what stays on the leg with what reaches the next flower.
gloss_pollination_definition: The transfer of pollen to a receptive part of a flower of the same plant species. Fertilization and seed development are later processes, and are not guaranteed by a flower visit.
gloss_pollination_here: Compare contact with missed contact in the final feeding step. A butterfly may sip nectar without delivering pollen.
gloss_pollinium_definition: A compact mass of pollen grains. Milkweed carries these masses in linked pairs called pollinaria; one mass can enter a receptive slit in another milkweed flower.
gloss_pollinium_here: Watch a milkweed visit to follow one enlarged pollen mass from the leg into a receiving slit while its partner remains carried.
gloss_prediction_definition: What you expect to happen, stated before you find out. A prediction that turns out wrong is still useful: it tells you your reasoning needs changing.
gloss_prediction_here: The planting, generation and seasonal investigations ask for one first, and record whether it matched.
gloss_proboscis_definition: The adult butterfly’s long, flexible drinking tube. It coils when not in use and uncoils to reach liquid food such as nectar.
gloss_proboscis_here: Choose Drinking tube close-up during a flower visit, then move Visit progress to inspect how the tube extends.
gloss_resource_definition: Something an organism needs and uses. Different stages of one species can need completely different resources.
gloss_resource_here: This lab tracks two: nectar for adults, and milkweed leaves for caterpillars.
gloss_stigma_definition: The receptive part of a flower where compatible pollen can begin germinating. Flower structures differ; milkweed receives a pollen packet through a specialized slit.
gloss_stigma_here: The pollen close-up shows the bergamot stigma or milkweed receiving slit. The contact comparison moves this surface outside the leg’s path.

lc_listen_why_milkweed: Milkweed holds bitter poisons called cardenolides. Monarch caterpillars store them in their bodies, and the adult butterflies keep them, so monarchs taste bad to many birds.
lc_listen_why_milkweed_simple: Milkweed has a bitter poison. Caterpillars keep the poison in their bodies, even after they become butterflies, so many birds learn that monarchs taste bad.
lc_why_milkweed: Milkweed holds bitter poisons called cardenolides. Monarch caterpillars store them in their bodies, and the adult butterflies keep them, so monarchs taste bad to many birds. Their bright colors are a warning: a bird that tastes one learns to avoid monarchs after that.
lc_why_milkweed_simple: Milkweed has a bitter poison. Caterpillars keep the poison in their bodies, even after they become butterflies, so many birds learn that monarchs taste bad. Their bright colors help birds remember.
lens_land_landed: Landed at {value1}. Examine this patch to record your evidence.
lens_land_move_closer: Move closer to a habitat patch before landing.
lens_note_bergamot_leaves: These are bergamot leaves. This plant offers adult nectar when flowering, but its leaves do not replace milkweed for monarch caterpillars.
lens_note_flowers: The highlighted flowers offer nectar to adult monarchs. Flowers are a feeding resource; seeing blooms does not tell you whether a plant can feed a monarch caterpillar.
lens_note_milkweed_leaf: The highlighted milkweed leaf is food for monarch caterpillars. Host plant means a plant that supports their feeding and development. Adults use flower nectar instead.
lens_note_no_flowers: This mown patch has grass but no flowers offering nectar. Its green appearance alone does not indicate an adult food source.
lens_note_no_milkweed: There is grass here, but no milkweed. Monarch caterpillars need milkweed leaves; green ground cover alone does not provide their host plant.
lens_observe_choose_plan: {value1} Choose a plan and make a prediction in the design activity to record a comparison.
lens_observe_land_first: Land at a habitat patch to examine it.
life_insp_feeding_note: The mouthparts close at the leaf edge, leaving small missing pieces. This enlarged sequence shows four illustrative bites, not a measured feeding rate or a complete meal. Rewind to compare the intact leaf with its bitten edge.
life_insp_maturation_note: {value1} This enlarged sequence illustrates visible changes before emergence; its progress does not measure elapsed time or show the hidden transformation inside.
life_insp_note_adult: Follow the orange wing surface, dark veins, and pale spots as the wings expand. This illustrative motion compresses emergence and expansion; real wings also need time to dry before flight.
life_insp_note_caterpillar: Look at the dark head capsule and its pale markings. Small mouthparts are near the front. This growth view shows the head, not individual bites or the five separate molts; choose Leaf feeding close-up to inspect the mouthparts at the leaf edge.
life_insp_note_caterpillar_blocked: The dark head has pale markings, but there is no milkweed here to eat. Inspecting or replaying this caterpillar cannot make it grow or form a chrysalis.
life_insp_note_chrysalis: A small silk pad and dark attachment support the hanging pupa. The green outer surface and gold markings are visible; the transformation into an adult happens out of sight inside.
life_insp_note_egg: The enlarged shell has fine lengthwise ribs. The egg does not feed; the developing caterpillar is hidden inside.
life_mat_note_green: The green case hides the developing adult. The pupa hangs from its attachment and does not feed.
life_mat_note_markings: As emergence approaches, the case becomes less opaque and the dark markings of the folded wings begin to show through.
life_mat_note_pattern: Orange and dark markings of the folded wings are visible through the case. The adult has not emerged or expanded its wings yet.
life_mat_note_unavailable: This close-up is available for the chrysalis of a generation supported by milkweed.
life_note_adult: The new adult emerges beside its empty case, then expands its wings. Real wings need time to expand and dry before flight; the short animation compresses that process.
life_note_caterpillar: The striped caterpillar eats milkweed. Hatching and growth through five instars are compressed into this step; its size change is illustrative.
life_note_caterpillar_blocked: The egg hatched, but this caterpillar has no milkweed to eat. Flower nectar cannot feed it. This model stops here; no chrysalis or adult forms.
life_note_chrysalis: The pupa hangs by a silk attachment while the adult develops inside. It does not feed. Real caterpillars often leave their food plant to find a sheltered pupation site.
life_note_egg: Look for the pale shell and its fine ribs. The egg does not feed. One enlarged egg represents the generation you are following.
life_title_egg_mown: An egg placed in the mown patch
life_uses_adult: Drinks flower nectar. This is the stage you fly.
life_uses_caterpillar: Eats milkweed leaves as it grows. Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed.
life_uses_chrysalis: Hangs from a support. It does not feed while it changes.
life_uses_egg: Laid on a milkweed leaf. It does not feed.
lw_caution: This is a model experiment on a non-host patch. Wild monarchs normally lay their eggs on milkweed. The model lets you compare what happens when that food is absent.

lw_model_note: One specimen represents the generation; sizes are enlarged. Development takes days to weeks, not seconds. Inspection controls do not advance the generation. Next stage changes the model; only Record saves the result.

src_note_experiments: In these experiments you place model eggs on any examined patch to test what happens; real female monarchs choose milkweed. An egg does not feed, so a patch without host leaves first blocks the feeding caterpillar stage. The mowing experiment keeps the chrysalis inside the patch and assumes cutting removes its support. Real caterpillars often leave their milkweed plant to find a secure place to pupate.
src_note_model_scope: Species: monarch (Danaus plexippus). This summer scene represents a Mid-Atlantic habitat investigation. Plants and wing patterns are illustrative and enlarged. Guided routes, flight speed, distances, and energy are teaching choices, not field measurements. The generation you follow is a teaching model of one outcome, not a population simulation: it turns on whether milkweed is present, and it deliberately leaves out weather, predators, parasites, disease, how many eggs are laid, and how many survive — all of which matter in a real meadow, where most eggs do not reach adulthood even on good milkweed. Real development also takes weeks and depends on temperature; the stages here advance when you choose, in a fixed order. Other butterfly species can have different host plants.
ssn_eyebrow: Time the mowing · Predict → Run → Compare
ssn_heading: Does it matter WHEN the patch is cut?
ssn_help_examine_first: Examine a patch in the meadow first. You can only run a season where you know what is growing.
ssn_help_run_no_change: Running a season does not change the plants. It only asks whether the plot is still standing when each stage needs it.
ssn_help_stage_days: Stage days are typical summer timing from Monarch Joint Venture; cool weather slows development, and real mowing dates vary by region. This activity models whether plants are present and still standing — not how many monarchs survive.
ssn_intro: A patch can hold the right plants and still lose the generation, if it is cut before a stage gets to use them. Run one patch under different mowing plans and compare.
ssn_intro_simple: A patch can have the right plants and still fail if it is mowed too soon. Try one patch with different mowing plans.
ssn_real_world: Mowers can kill monarch eggs, caterpillars and chrysalises. Monarch Joint Venture advises land managers to avoid mowing habitat while monarchs are present, to mow less often, and not to mow a whole habitat at once.
ssn_real_world_simple: Mowers can kill monarch eggs, caterpillars and chrysalises. Experts say: do not mow while monarchs are there, mow less often, and leave some areas unmowed.
ssn_real_world_source: Source: Monarch Joint Venture, mowing and management best practices
